## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. ## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Game 1 — Black versus 9d

Result: White wins by resignation after White 40 J4. Captures: Black 0, White 6. Exact record: game-001.sgf. No external engine analysis was used; conclusions below are manual and do not establish optimal alternatives.

Opening: B E5, W C4; B F3, W D6; B F6, W E8. Black intended to develop the right and center, while White took the left/top. B7 F8 attached on the second line without checking how the stone would escape. W8 F7 and later W16 G8 left it isolated. B17 F9 and B19 G9 expanded the trapped first-line chain. It remained in atari at the end, with H9 its sole liberty. Better future practice: assess liberties and connection routes before an edge attachment; do not repeatedly invest in a chain without a viable exit.

Black invaded C7 at move 25 and followed B7/C8. The corner had room, but its life was not established. Do not record this invasion as confirmed alive or successful.

Decisive fight: W30 G6 cut between Black F6 and G7. B31 H6, W32 G5; B33 G4, W34 H5. At this point the four-stone Black chain G7-H7-J7-H6 had only J6 as a liberty. B35 J5 did not remove its atari. White instead played G2. B37 J6 joined that chain to J5, but the resulting six-stone group had only J4 as a liberty. White played F2. Black wrongly believed the connection was safe and played B39 H4; W40 J4 captured all six stones.

The exact distinct-liberty sets matter: before B39 H4, the six-stone upper-right group had {J4}, while White's G6-G5-H5 group had {F5,H4}. B39 H4 put the White group in atari at F5, but left Black's larger group in atari at J4. White captured first, opening several liberties for its own stones. This was not a successful attack.

Primary lesson: a connection can preserve atari. Count the merged group's external liberties, excluding occupied connecting points and counting shared empty points only once. Attacking a neighboring group does not protect your own group if the opponent can capture it immediately.

Training for game 2: use explicit liberty counts every turn; fix endangered groups before new invasions; play against an easier profile if useful to practice complete games and area scoring. Avoid claiming a move is best from this single unreviewed loss. Record recurring errors and results so progress can be measured.

# Game 3 — Black versus 20k

Result: White wins by 16 points (W+16), after B45 pass and W46 pass. First completed scored game in the series; no win demonstrated at 20k. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: 0 for both players. Exact record: game-003.sgf. No engine analysis, move-ranking code, or sequence-search program was used. Existing-group distinct liberties were inspected after every opponent reply; strategic judgments below are manual, not established optimal play.

Opening: B E5/G3/G7, followed by G2/G4/F4/F5. White took C7 and built along D4–D6, with F1–F3 below. Black extended E6/E7/D7/D8/D9 while White connected C6/C8/C9. This built a connected Black boundary but also let White develop much of the left side. B25 F7 joined G7 to the main chain. W26 H2 entered the lower right; B27 H3 and B29 J3 blocked upward expansion, but W30 H1 connected the invasion to the bottom White stones. The right-side space alone did not win with komi. Future practice: assess the territorial balance while developing; repeatedly answering local boundary moves can leave too little elsewhere. This record does not prove an optimal opening replacement.

Failed invasion: B31 C3 had four liberties {B3,C2,C4,D3}, but no eyes. W32 D2 restricted the bottom. B33 C4 extended toward White D4; W34 C2 removed the lower liberty. B35 C5 extended toward White C6/D5. W36 B3 left the three-stone chain with {B4,B5,D3}. It had no established eye space and no clear exit. Recognizing danger only here was too late to establish a rescue in this game.

B37 B5, W38 B6 left {A5,B4,D3}. B39 B4 joined internally but still left only {A4,A5,D3}; it did not improve the liberty count or establish eyes. W40 B2 joined White B3 to C2/D2, removing the prospect of capturing an isolated B3 stone easily. B41 A5 left {A4,A6,D3}. W42 D3 joined White's upper and lower chains, leaving Black only {A4,A6}. B43 A6 filled one liberty and gained A7; W44 A7 left seven Black stones {A5,A6,B4,B5,C3,C4,C5} in atari at A4. A4 would leave only A3, still without eyes or an exit. Black passed, and White passed; the scorer returned W+16 with those stones still on the board. No explicit dead-stone breakdown was returned.

The main right-side chain had ten distinct liberties at the end: {E8,E9,F6,F8,G5,G6,G8,H4,H7,J4}. Its safety was not the decisive failure. The seven-stone invasion was recognized as lost before passing; unlike game 1, its atari was not overlooked.

Lessons for game 4:

- Liberty counting worked as observation, but did not prevent enclosure. A four-liberty invasion can have poor prospects if extensions lead toward enemy strength and there is no plan for two eyes or an exit.
- Before invading, identify usable living space and how the opponent can block access to it. C3's open-looking corner was restricted immediately by D2/C2 and then B3.
- Reassess after each restricting reply. By W34 C2, Black had four liberties but only leftward space; B35 C5 added stones toward the strong upper White chain rather than widening living space.
- Do not equate connecting or maintaining three liberties with progress. B39 B4 left the same count and reduced interior room; A5/A6 repeated the earlier games' edge-running pattern.
- Avoid investing more stones in an enclosure just to prolong atari. A rescue needs a concrete capture, eye-space improvement, or exit.
- Keep a rough area balance in mind before the board is partitioned. Securing one side can still be insufficient with White's komi and lower-right gains.
- Passing was appropriate only after checking that the endangered group had no identified rescue and the remaining boundary had no identified profitable move. This manual assessment is not an engine-certified claim.

Next training recommendation: stay at 20k. Aim to establish eye space before enclosure and finish another scored game, seeking an actual win before increasing rank. Ultimate target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 4 — White versus 20k

Second scored game; still no demonstrated win at 20k. Current-position group/liberty inspection was used after every opponent board move. No engine analysis, move-ranking program, or future-sequence search was used. Strategic conclusions are manual and do not establish optimal alternatives.

However, the plan was only 'there is room to develop eyes', not an identified pair of usable eye regions. B43 H2 immediately took the route toward the bottom corner. W44 H4 and W46 H5 expanded upward. B47 G4 restricted the left. W48 G5, B49 F5; W50 G6, B51 F6. Black F6 joined the row-7 chain to the large central/lower chain, removing the prospect of an easy capture above. White's right group then had {G3,H6,J3,J4,J5}: five liberties, no established eyes. This was the critical reassessment point.

W52 H6 expanded toward the top edge, but B53 D6 left the surrounding Black chain with six liberties. W54 J3 and B55 G2 joined Black H2 to that chain. W56 J2, B57 H1 blocked the bottom route. The eight White stones {G5,G6,H3,H4,H5,H6,J2,J3} finished with {G3,J1,J4,J5,J6}. G3 bordered Black F3/G4/G2; J1 bordered Black H1; J6 bordered Black J7. These were liberties, not enclosed White eyes. The scorer returned B+10 without a dead-stone breakdown, so the exact automatic treatment of the right group was not separately reported.

Lessons for game 5:

- Preserve the successful outside connection pattern: C2 joined the lower group while leaving the captured point D3 as an eye. Connection and eye space should be checked separately.
- Before a new isolated group, name two potential eye regions and identify the opponent's moves that could remove them. Open points near an edge are not automatically usable living space.
- Reassess immediately after a reply takes one of those regions. B43 H2 removed the bottom-corner route; B51 F6 connected the enclosing chains. Continuing merely because the group had five liberties repeated the central error of games 2 and 3.
- For each candidate eye point, check all orthogonal neighbors. A liberty bordering a strong enemy chain is not an enclosed eye. Adjacent empty points such as J4/J5 usually form one eye region, not two eyes.
- Plan area balance earlier. White's upper and lower-left holdings together were roughly 32 area points; komi brought that to 39 against approximately 49 if Black controlled the remainder. That rough count matched the final margin, but does not prove a precise dead-stone breakdown. Earlier broader development might avoid needing a late isolated group; no optimal replacement move is established here.
- Five liberties can coexist with a strategically lost enclosure. Recognize that before atari and avoid adding stones solely to prolong it.

Next training recommendation: remain at 20k and seek a scored win before increasing rank. Aim to develop connected frameworks with usable eye space and count rough area before the board is partitioned. The long-term target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 2 — White versus 12k

Result: Black wins by resignation after B45 J9. White captured one stone; Black captured none before resignation. The 17-stone upper White group was in atari at C8 and could not save itself. Exact record: game-002.sgf (45 board moves; resignation is in RE[B+R]). Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. No engine analysis or sequence-search program was used. Current-position liberty counting was used before every White move.

Progress: the final atari was correctly recognized, unlike game 1. However, counting liberties did not prevent a larger strategic group-safety failure. No demonstrated winning strength at 12k and still no completed scored game.

Opening and shape: White took C3/C6 and expanded through D7/D6/E7/E8. Black's B5–E5 chain separated White's upper and lower groups, while F7/F8 and then F6 restricted the upper group on the right. White's B7/B8/B6 responses to A7/A8/A6 connected the upper stones, but Black A5 joined its edge invasion to the central chain. The invasion was not captured. White's upper group had six liberties after W22 B6, but little enclosed space and no demonstrated two-eye life.

Critical contraction: after W24 E6 B25 F6, the upper group had {B9,C7,C8,D8,E9}. B29 B9 removed B9. W30 C9 created a separate two-liberty group; W32 D9 expanded that group, but B33 C8 invaded the remaining interior. Before W34 D8, the main upper group had {C7,D8,E9}, the C9–D9 pair had {D8,E9}, and Black C8 had {C7,D8}. W34 D8 joined the White groups but left only {C7,E9}; Black C8 was in atari at C7. Lessons for game 3:

- Count distinct liberties, then separately check where two eyes or an actual exit can come from. A group with several liberties can already have inadequate living space.
- Before filling an interior liberty to connect, check the merged group's liberties AND remaining eye space. W34 D8 was the clearest warning: two liberties, no established eyes, surrounded externally.

- Repeated first-line extensions that keep the same two-liberty count are a danger signal. The F9–H9 chase repeated game 1's edge-trapping error on a larger scale.

Next training recommendation: 20k or 18k, White or Black as the user specifies, with the aim of preserving eye space and finishing a scored game. Increase rank only on demonstrated results. Keep the ultimate target of consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 6 — White versus 20k

Result: Black wins by 26 points (B+26), after W56 pass and B57 pass. Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. Captures before scoring: White 2, Black 0. Exact record: game-006.sgf. Fourth scored game; no win yet at any rank. Current-position distinct liberties were counted after every opponent board move. No engine analysis, move-ranking code, or future-sequence search was used. Tactical and strategic conclusions below are manual.

Opening: W2 C3 and W4 C6 took the left; W6 D7, W8 D6 built upward while Black occupied E5/E3/G6/E7. W10 C4, W12 D4, W14 D5 connected the left boundary. B15 D8 capped the upper route. This was recognized before entering the lower right, yet the new group's life plan remained too vague.

Lower-right failure: W18 G3 was earlier than game 4's invasion, with open bottom and corner space. However, those directions were not independently secured eye regions. W20 H3, B21 F3; W22 G2, B23 F2; W24 G1, B25 J2. White answered the invasion with W26 J3 and W28 H2; B29 J1 left Black J1/J2 in atari at H1. W30 H1 correctly captured both stones. W32 F1, B33 E1 left eight White stones {F1,G1,G2,G3,H1,H2,H3,J3} with {J1,J2}, no exit and no second eye. White correctly stopped adding stones then, but recognized the enclosure too late. Playing inside the two-point region would reduce the group's liberties to one; no capture or rescue was identified.

Left boundary completion: W34 C7, W36 B7, W38 A7 were answered by C8/B8/A8. W40 C2, W42 B2, W44 A2, W46 A1 closed the bottom boundary against C1/B1/D1. The final 15-stone left chain had {A3,A6,B3,B4,B6,C5}, with a broad connected interior behind it. Preserving that space was useful, but this framework occupied only roughly 24 area points, far short of a winning share even with komi.

Second failed entry: After B47 G7, White reconsidered passing because the upper right was open. W48 H8 had three liberties after B49 G8, and W50 H7 still had three after B51 H6: {H9,J7,J8}. Those were already a narrow corridor, not two secured eye regions. W52 J7, B53 J6 left {H9,J8}; W54 H9, B55 G9 left four stones {H7,H8,H9,J7} with {J8,J9}. Again these were one adjacent two-point eye region with no exit. The proposed top/right living areas overlapped and Black sealed their boundaries in successive replies. White passed rather than fill the remaining region; Black passed.

The scorer returned B+26 without a dead-stone breakdown. A rough partition of 24 White area versus 57 Black area gives the same margin with komi 7, but this is a consistency check, not an explicit report of how each group was adjudicated.

Lessons for game 7:

- Naming two directions is insufficient. Name two DISTINCT potential eye regions and the boundary points required to preserve each. Bottom and corner space in the lower right collapsed into the same J1/J2 region.
- A capture can be tactically correct while the group remains strategically enclosed. After W30 H1, explicitly count eyes separately from liberties: three liberties, one eye region, and only F1 as an external route.
- Check closure threats before answering an interior invasion. J2 diverted moves while Black F2/F3/G4 and later E1 sealed the outside. This record does not prove an optimal alternative, but the assessment must happen before the enclosure is complete.
- Reassess a new group after its FIRST restrictive reply. After B49 G8 and especially B51 H6, the upper-right group's three liberties did not imply adequate living space. H7/J7 extended a narrow boundary without securing eyes.
- Do not repeat a failed corner pattern elsewhere in the same game. Both right groups finished with exactly one two-point eye region.
- Maintain the successful connected boundary and open interior, but contest a larger share earlier. By B15 D8, the left framework was capped; continuing local development could not supply enough area.
- Liberty counting is now exposing failures accurately, but must change decisions earlier. Another completed loss is not evidence of improved playing strength.

Next training recommendation: remain at 20k. Aim for an actual scored win through early area balance and groups with distinct usable eye space or checked outside connections. Ultimate target remains consistent wins against 9d.

# Game 5 — Black versus 20k

W10 E4 and W12 E3 expanded toward the bottom, but B13 F2 and B15 E2 restricted that direction. White switched to D7/E7/F7 above Black's center. The upper chain retained the connected empty region E8/E9/F9/G9/H9/J9 at the finish. Do not fill this region simply because it is a liberty. White's H5/H6 then had {J5,J6}, and J7 had {J6,J8}. W52 J8 joined J7 to the upper White chain, with seven liberties. B53 J5 put H5/H6 in atari at J6. W54 J6 joined the WHOLE upper group to those two stones and left six liberties, all in the upper interior. This checked connection avoided another isolated-group loss. function inspectLiberties(boardText) {
  const columns = 'ABCDEFGHJ';
  const cells = new Map();
  for (const line of boardText.split('\n')) {
    const m = line.match(/^\s*([1-9])\s+([XO.](?:\s+[XO.]){8})\s+[1-9]\s*$/);
    if (m) m[2].split(/\s+/).forEach((v, x) => cells.set(columns[x] + m[1], v));
  }
  if (cells.size !== 81) throw new Error('Expected a complete 9x9 text board');
  function neighbors(p) {
    const x = columns.indexOf(p[0]), y = Number(p[1]);
    return [[x-1,y],[x+1,y],[x,y-1],[x,y+1]]
      .filter(([a,b]) => a >= 0 && a < 9 && b >= 1 && b <= 9)
      .map(([a,b]) => columns[a]+b);
  }
  const seen = new Set(), groups = [];
  for (const [point, color] of cells) {
    if (color === '.' || seen.has(point)) continue;
    const stones = [], liberties = new Set(), stack = [point];
    seen.add(point);
    while (stack.length) {
      const p = stack.pop(); stones.push(p);
      for (const q of neighbors(p)) {
        if (cells.get(q) === '.') liberties.add(q);
        else if (cells.get(q) === color && !seen.has(q)) {
          seen.add(q); stack.push(q);
        }
      }
    }
    groups.push({ color, stones: stones.sort(), liberties: [...liberties].sort(), count: liberties.size });
  }
  return groups;
}
